reasons: Opened: Egill Hofudlausn st. 'Ber ek Odin-mjod a engla bjod ... Hljods bidjum hann'; RV 4.38.10d 'prnaktu madhva sam ima vacamsi'. mjodr : madhu- < *medhu- is sound (Kroonen *medu-). But there is no congruent collocation: Norse mead = poetry via the Kvasir/poetic-mead myth (a kenning, mead carried/offered), Vedic asks that words be mixed with honey (honeyed speech). Only one cognate element, the verbs and syntax differ. Honey-sweet speech is cross-culturally common and also Near Eastern (Ps 119:103, Prov 16:24), so the figure is at best a loose thematic parallel.
known: Mead/honey of poetry and honeyed words are widely discussed (Kvasir-Soma comparisons since Dumezil; poetic mead/honeyed speech in West, IEPM).

reasons: Opened: Thidreks saga 'brennr oc gloar sva mitt hiarta sem thetta gull gloar' (speaker's own heart burning with eagerness); RV 10.34.9d dice like coals 'hrdayam nis dahanti'; RV 10.103.12c 'nis daha hrtsu sokaih' (against enemies); AVP 12.21.2 'dvisatah tapayan hrdah'. Heart cognate (*kerd-, Kroonen *herton-) is fine but is the only shared element; verbs not cognate, agents and transitivity differ (intransitive emotional burning vs. burning/heating others' hearts). Fire-as-emotion is near-universal and the Norse text is a translated/adapted chivalric saga with biblical heart-burning available. Generic.

Opened: Egill 'Hljods bidjum hann'; Voluspa 1 'Hljods bid ek allar kindir meiri ok minni'; Y 45.1 'at frauuaxsiia nu gusodum nu sraota / yaeca asnat yaeca durat'. Etymology sound: hljod < *hleutha- < *klew-to-, which Kroonen equates with Av. sraota- n. 'listening'; the Gathic form here is the verb sraota (2pl imper.), so the shape is renewed (noun object of 'ask' vs imperative). Context truly comparable (poet's opening call for a hearing before solemn recitation), and Voluspa's merism of addressees (greater and lesser) parallels Gathic near and far. But *klew- is simply the basic 'hear' root, a call for attention is a generic poetic opening, and ON kvedja ser hljods is an everyday assembly idiom.
known: Call for attention/hearing (klew-) at poem opening is a recognized IE poetic topos (West, IEPM; Watkins on Gathic/Vedic 'hear!').

reasons: Opened: Thidreks saga 'gengom ... firir ydr ... ok stondum nu firir ydrum kniom' (surrendering townsmen); Il. 11.609-610 'peri gounat' ema stesesthai Akhaious lissomenous'. Two cognates (*steh2-, *genu-) in a congruent supplication/surrender context, which is better than knee-grasping alone. But the prepositions differ (before vs around), the knee-supplication gesture is widespread (also Hittite and Near Eastern), and the Norse source is a 13th-c. saga adapted from German material with medieval courtly submission ritual; 'stand before X's knees' can arise from the gesture itself.
known: Knee supplication (gounata, genu-) is well known in the literature on IE/Greek supplication; this specific standing variant not known to me.

reasons: Opened: Thidreks saga 'mærkr af raudo gulli'; bylina 'Pryazhki u sedla da krasna zolota ... Krasno zoloto ne rzhavfet' (stock saddling formula). gull : zoloto cognate (*ghel-), but rauðr and krasnyj are not cognate and krasnyj meant 'beautiful' originally, so 'krasnoe zoloto' is not even semantically 'red' gold in origin. 'Red gold' is a common medieval Germanic and Slavic epithet (areal/natural); contexts (gift vs non-rusting buckles) differ. Generic.

Opened: MLL 'ef that kømr lifi i ljos ok verdr skirt' (inheritance of a child born alive and baptised); Lucr. 1.170 'oras in luminis exit', 2.617 'uiuam progeniem qui in oras luminis edant', 5.224-225 'in luminis oras nixibus ex aluo matris natura profudit'. ljos (< *leuk-s-, Kroonen) and lumen (< *leuk-, de Vaan s.v. lux) share the root but not the formation; one element only, verbs renewed. Birth as coming into the light is natural (also Gk phaosde), and the Norse is a 13th-c. royal law code in a baptism clause, where Latin legal/learned 'in lucem edi/venire' is a ready model. The 'alive' element (lifi / uiuam) is a nice but semantically automatic match.
known: Birth/life as (coming into) the light, Lat. in luminis oras (Ennius), Gk phaosde, discussed in West, IEPM.

reasons: Opened: Thidreks saga 'hans nafn mun aldrigi tynaz i thydværskri tungo oc slict sama med nordmannom'; Theognis 245-246 'oude thanon apoleis kleos ... aphthiton anthropois aien ekhon onoma'. nafn : onoma sound (*h1nomn-). The Greek actually also has a negated loss verb (apoleis kleos), closer than the lead says, though with kleos, not onoma. Still only one cognate; 'his name will never be forgotten/lost' is a pan-medieval and biblical commonplace (Ps 72:17 nomen eius in saecula) and Near Eastern ('establish a name forever'), and the saga is adapted from German sources. Commemoration context is comparable.
known: Imperishable fame (aphthiton kleos = aksiti sravas) and its ON echo (ordstirr deyr aldrigi, Havamal 76-77) are classic; the name-variant here is part of that discussion.

reasons: Opened: AM 178 fol 'ei meira nafnn bera enn ...' (will not bear a greater title); Eur. Hel. 66 'onoma dyskleès phero'. Exact cognate pair bera : phero (*bher-) + nafn : onoma (*h1nomn-) as verb + object; Kroonen confirms nafn. But the senses differ (holding a title vs bearing a reputation), the Norse is late paper-manuscript prose, and 'bear a name' is an easy metaphor also in Latin (nomen ferre/gerere), from which medieval Norse could calque. See L011 for the stronger three-branch version.

Opened: Thidreks saga 'hvargi theirra ma af adrom bera sigr'; Hymn. Hom. 6.19-20 'dos d' en agoni niken tode pheresthai'. Only *bher- is shared, the most generic 'carry' verb, and 'carry off victory/prize' is a natural expression found also in Latin (victoriam ferre/reportare) and later European languages; victory nouns unrelated, voice and context (combat vs song contest) differ. Generic.

Opened: MLB (Magnus' law, Christmas peace) 'med ordum eda verkum'; Il. 5.879 'ou t' epei ... oute ti ergo', Il. 11.703 'epeon ... ede kai ergon'. verk : ergon (*werg-) cognate, speech member not. 'In word or deed' is a universal merism and a fixed Christian/Latin legal formula (verbo vel facto, cogitatione verbo et opere), which a 13th-c. Norwegian law code most plausibly reflects. One element only, high derivative risk.
known: Word-and-deed merism (epos/ergon) is a well-known Homeric polar expression, discussed in IE merism literature.

reasons: Opened all: RV 5.30.5b 'srutyam nama bibhrat', 1.103.4b 'kirtenyam ... nama bibhrat', 9.109.14a 'bibharti caru indrasya nama' (8 RV instances of nama + bhar- confirmed in corpus); Eur. Hel. 66; Soph. OC 60 'pherousi tounoma'; ON AM-36 'bera tignar nafn', Laxdæla 'beri thræls nafn'. Exact cognate verb-object pair (*bher- + *h1nomn-) in the same sense 'bear/hold a name or title', often with an evaluative modifier, in three branches; ON usage is native prose. Defensible as inherited, but the metaphor is easily formed independently and also in Latin (nomen ferre/gerere) and Biblical idiom, so not compelling.
known: Ved. nama bhar- / Gk onoma pherein may have been compared in the IE name literature; I cannot confirm a specific citation, and know of none for the ON member.

reasons: Opened: Thidreks saga 'nu er lypt thvi oci af minum halsi er a hævir lægit hinn riki Villcinus konungr' with tribute; Theognis 1023-1024 'hypo zygon aukhena theso dyslophon'; Aesch. Pers. 594 'elythe zygon alkas'. ok : zygon (*yugom) cognate, neck nouns not. The political yoke-on-the-neck metaphor is quintessentially Biblical (Gen 27:40, Isa 10:27, Jer 28) and Near Eastern (Assyrian 'yoke of my lordship'), so it is areal, and the Norse romance most plausibly takes it from Latin/Christian usage. One element only; derivative.
known: Yoke of servitude is a well-known Near Eastern/Biblical figure; not a recognized specifically IE formula.
